material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Solvent S and extractant X are independent benchmark labels, not real substance identities. Equal indices across the two fields imply no shared identity or property. The catalog provides no material-property estimates.

dossier.identity_policy: Solvent and extractant IDs are independent benchmark-only labels and do not identify real materials. Equal codes across the two fields have no meaning.
dossier.interpretation_policy: Treat the marginal profiles as incomplete prior evidence. They cannot identify the best pair without controlled pairwise experiments and do not reveal the objective score or optimal process settings.

property_scope.extractant: Marginal nominal distribution and selectivity tendencies aggregated across an anonymous solvent reference panel.
property_scope.solvent: Marginal nominal distribution and selectivity tendencies aggregated across an anonymous extractant reference panel.

dossier.residual_policy: The solvent-extractant interaction table, world-level coefficient transform, phase-volume response, and mixing response are not disclosed. The hidden law is fixed for the entire campaign.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

notes.text:
# Partition hypotheses (source stage)

## H1 [tentative; prediction before experiments]
At a fixed phase-volume ratio and adequate mixing/settling, target phase fractions will depend on the solvent–extractant pairing rather than on matching anonymous indices. The dossier suggests S2 and X0 have relatively favorable marginal target distribution, but pair interactions remain unresolved. A pre-separation HPLC should show organic and aqueous fractions whose sum is near the recoverable inventory, subject to sampling/noise.

## H2 [tentative; prediction before experiments]
Increasing organic fraction should increase the batch fraction of target in the organic phase according to a finite distribution relationship, while the underlying concentration ratio may remain approximately pair-specific. This will be tested with repeated material pairs at different phase amounts.

## H3 [tentative; prediction before experiments]
Mixing has a threshold/saturation role: insufficient mixing may reduce apparent equilibration, whereas increases beyond adequate mixing should have smaller effects. Separation removes a phase, so final assay after retaining organic versus aqueous should primarily report the retained inventory and cannot substitute for the pre-separation two-phase HPLC.

Planned scope: 12 independent batches, one pre-separation HPLC per batch and one required final assay, spanning material pair, organic fraction, mixing intensity/duration, and both retention decisions. Numerical differences will be treated cautiously given declared instrument/process noise and limited replication.

# Partition hypotheses (source stage)

## H1 [supported in tested scope; pairing effects remain only sparsely mapped]
At comparable phase additions and moderate mixing, anonymous material choice changes target partition; matching indices have no assumed meaning. With X0, S0 gave the weakest organic target fraction (0.290; event runner-operation-0027), while S1 and S3 gave about 0.499 and 0.514 (runner-operation-0037, -0047). With S2, X3 gave 0.502 versus 0.417–0.437 for X1/X2 and 0.399/0.428 in two X0 batches (runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0057, -0067, -0077). Approximate concentration-ratio proxies D=(f_org/r)/(f_aq/(1-r)) range from about 1.6 for S0/X0 to 4.9 for S2/X3. These are numerical contrasts with sparse replication; pair interaction is unresolved because the full 4x4 matrix was not measured.

## H2 [unresolved / volume intervention weak in this scope]
The intended high- versus low-organic-addition comparison did not create a clearly ordered observed phase-ratio shift: HPLC phase_ratio was 0.194 after 0.06 L solvent + 0.02 L aqueous and 0.209 after 0.02 L solvent + 0.06 L aqueous (runner-operation-0087, -0097). Both are within the spread of nominally fixed-addition batches (roughly 0.17–0.22). Because initial liquid and all additions contribute to actual volumes, the tested 0.04 L redistribution was likely small relative to total phase volumes and batch/process variation. Thus a finite-distribution volume law is plausible but not established. A stronger test would directly span phase_ratio while holding pairing/mixing fixed and replicate endpoints.

## H3 [supported directionally; threshold not located]
Mixing affected partition strongly at S2/X0: 5 s at 100 rpm produced organic/aqueous fractions 0.345/0.648 (runner-operation-0107), whereas 1200 s at 1200 rpm produced 0.510/0.516 (runner-operation-0117). Moderate-mix repeats were intermediate but variable (runner-operation-0007, -0017). This supports mass-transfer/equilibration limitation at very low mixing, but duration and speed were changed together, so their separate roles and the saturation threshold remain unresolved.

## H4 [supported phase-retention interpretation]
Pre-separation HPLC measured both phases; final assays after separation behaved as retained-inventory checks rather than alternate sampling. Organic-retention assays approximately reproduced the earlier organic fraction and showed little aqueous target (e.g. runner-operation-0047 to -0050). Aqueous-retention assays approximately reproduced the aqueous fraction and little organic target (e.g. runner-operation-0057 to -0060). Across the tested conditions, organic-retained material had much lower impurity signal (~0.01–0.04) and higher purity (~0.93–0.95) than aqueous-retained material (impurity ~0.22–0.25, purity ~0.67–0.73), supporting preferential impurity residence in the aqueous phase. Small nonzero removed-phase readings and imperfect closure are treated as sampling/noise, not literal remaining inventory.

## Limits and next tests
Only one or two measurements occupy most factor combinations, initial-mixture volume is not directly observed, phase-ratio noise/process variation is appreciable, and material and mixing effects were not fully crossed. No missing reading is interpreted as zero. Future blind predictions should therefore use pair-specific D only as a rough local descriptor, include broader uncertainty for untested pairings/phase ratios, and condition retention predictions on whether target recovery or purity is the queried outcome.

payload.report:
Observations

Twelve batches were completed with one pre-separation HPLC measurement and one post-separation final assay per batch. The common reference preparation used 0.020 mol reagent, 0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L added aqueous phase, 0.020 L extractant, mixing for 300 s at 600 rpm, and settling for 300 s.

Material pairing mattered under those reference conditions. With X0, the measured organic target fraction was 0.290 for S0 (batch 3; runner-operation-0027), 0.499 for S1 (batch 4; -0037), 0.399 and 0.428 in two S2/X0 batches (batches 1–2; -0007 and -0017), and 0.514 for S3 (batch 5; -0047). Holding S2 and changing the extractant gave organic fractions of 0.437 with X1, 0.417 with X2, and 0.502 with X3 (batches 6–8; -0057, -0067, and -0077). Thus neither matching solvent/extractant indices nor selecting materials solely by their marginal dossier rankings predicted the observed ordering.

Mixing produced the clearest process contrast. At S2/X0, 5 s at 100 rpm gave organic/aqueous target fractions of 0.345/0.648 (batch 11; -0107), whereas 1200 s at 1200 rpm gave 0.510/0.516 (batch 12; -0117). The moderate-mixing S2/X0 batches were intermediate, although variable.

The volume intervention was not decisive. Changing the additions from 0.060 L solvent plus 0.020 L aqueous phase to 0.020 L solvent plus 0.060 L aqueous phase yielded measured phase ratios of 0.194 and 0.209 and organic target fractions of 0.424 and 0.431, respectively (batches 9–10; -0087 and -0097). This small, oppositely ordered difference is not persuasive evidence of the expected phase-amount effect.

The retention assays strongly identify which inventory followed each phase. In every organic-retention batch, the final organic target estimate was close to the earlier HPLC organic estimate—for example 0.514 before separation and 0.519 afterward in batch 5 (-0047 to -0050). Aqueous retention behaved analogously—for example 0.603 before and 0.608 afterward in batch 2 (-0017 to -0020). Across six examples of each decision, organic-retained material generally had impurity signals near 0.01–0.04 and purity near 0.93–0.95, whereas aqueous-retained material had impurity near 0.22–0.25 and purity near 0.67–0.73. Small signals assigned to the removed phase and imperfect closure were also observed.

Inference

A useful local account is finite partition between the phases, with a pairing-dependent preference for the organic phase and a mixing-dependent approach to that partition. Using the reported phase ratio as an organic-volume fraction, an approximate concentration-ratio proxy spans about 1.6 for S0/X0 to about 4.9 for S2/X3. This indicates organic preference in all tested pairs but substantial pair-specific strength. It is only a descriptive proxy, not a precisely fitted law: the two nominal S2/X0 repeats imply values of roughly 2.5 and 3.6.

The low-mixing result is consistent with mass-transfer limitation, while vigorous mixing moves more target into the organic phase. The experiment does not locate an equilibration threshold. The final assays further imply that the impurity preferentially accompanies the aqueous phase, so retaining organic favors purity while retaining aqueous preserves the target portion remaining there.

Supplied information versus experimental contribution

The supplied dossier provided useful priors: it suggested generally organic-favoring target distributions, identified S2 and X0 as promising marginal materials, and warned that solvent–extractant interactions and process responses were undisclosed. It could not select a pair. The experiments supplied the decisive pairing evidence, showed that S1/X0, S3/X0, and S2/X3 outperformed the observed S2/X0 reference in organic target fraction, revealed the strong mixing contrast, and validated phase retention directly. The failed volume contrast was also informative because it limits how strongly phase-amount behavior can be claimed from this campaign.

Competing explanations and uncertain scope

Most material combinations were measured once, and only S2/X0 had a reference repeat, whose variation was appreciable. Some apparent material rankings may therefore reflect batch/process variation rather than stable pair effects. The full 4×4 pairing matrix was not studied, so solvent and extractant main effects cannot be separated reliably from interactions.

Mixing speed and duration were changed together; either variable, their combined energy input, or another correlated process effect could explain the contrast. Although mass transfer is the leading interpretation, altered formation or loss of measurable target is a competing explanation.

The phase-amount test changed additions but did not generate a large, clean change in measured phase ratio, possibly because pre-existing liquid dominated total phase volumes or because the tested range was too narrow. Consequently, the functional dependence on phase amounts and extrapolation to substantially different ratios remain unresolved.

Finally, the purity difference after retention could include matrix, entrainment, or assay-basis effects in addition to true impurity partition. Consistency across retention replicates supports the qualitative conclusion, but the small removed-phase signals and imperfect mass-balance closure argue against interpreting any single estimate as exact.

payload.rationale: I treated extractant volume relative to the combined solvent-plus-aqueous volume as the phase-amount driver, used the measured pair-specific concentration preferences, and interpolated the observed increase with mixing intensity and duration. Q01 remains aqueous-majority because its extractant fraction is small. X3 exceeded X0 with S2 experimentally, but S0/X3 was never tested and the supplied marginal information favors X0, so the strongly overlapping Q05–Q06 intervals make that comparison uncertain.

payload.report:
1. The least-supported self-developed law is the phase-volume model used in the predictions: I treated extractant volume relative to the other liquid volumes as the organic-phase fraction and combined it with a pair-specific distribution coefficient. Batches 9 and 10 did not establish that relationship—their deliberately changed solvent/aqueous additions produced nearly identical HPLC results (runner-operation-0087 and -0097). The mixing law is also only provisional because duration and speed changed together between batches 11 and 12. No separate instance-specific prior was supplied; the supplied dossier contained only incomplete marginal material properties, not the hidden pair interaction or process law.

2. I would run one S2/X0 batch at fixed phase amounts and use a within-batch staged-mixing test: mix for 120 s at 700 rpm, settle and measure both target fractions by HPLC, then remix the same batch at 700 rpm to 1200 s cumulative time, settle and measure again. The mass-transfer explanation predicts a reproducible rise in organic target fraction with approximately conserved organic-plus-aqueous target inventory. Little change would favor batch variation or rapid equilibration over a duration effect. A changing total target inventory, impurity signal, or purity accompanying the redistribution would increase support for mixing-dependent target formation/loss or another chemical-process explanation rather than simple partition kinetics.

3. The final retention assays were underused in the numerical predictions: across the organic- and aqueous-retention batches they supplied repeated checks on phase assignment and mass recovery, although they did not directly determine new pre-separation fractions. I also underused the dossier’s marginal geometric means and variability information, and I did not formally pool the S2/X0 repeats or propagate the observed process variability into a fitted uncertainty model.

The least reliable predictions are Q03, Q04, and Q06 because S0/X3 was never measured; Q08, Q11, and Q12 because S2/X3 was observed at only one mixing condition; and Q09–Q10 because they require separating duration from speed despite their being confounded in the campaign. Q01–Q04 also extrapolate to extractant volumes outside the tested 0.019–0.020 L neighborhood.

There is a real tension between the sealed report and predictions. The report explicitly classified the phase-amount dependence as unresolved, but the predictions nevertheless imposed a specific finite-partition volume rule. The report also warned that pair interactions were sparsely mapped, while the point estimates extrapolated the X3 advantage observed with S2 to the untested S0/X3 pair. The broad overlapping intervals and the “uncertain” Q05-versus-Q06 decision acknowledged these weaknesses, but they do not turn those assumptions into experimentally supported laws.
